title: Getting Candidates to Talk About Their Weaknesses
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece is a tactical guide for interviewers trying to get past candidates' rehearsed, strength-disguised-as-weakness answers. The author names the common evasion pattern and offers several reframed questions designed to surface honest self-assessment, such as asking what a candidate's friends or colleagues would say are their least favorable qualities. The technique's core mechanism is projection, candidates are more willing to voice unflattering truths when framed as someone else's observation. The piece frames genuinely understanding a candidate's weaknesses as essential to an accurate hiring assessment.
points: Candidates routinely disguise a strength as a weakness in interviews, which the piece names as a predictable evasion pattern to watch for.
Asking candidates to speak from the vantage point of someone who knows them well makes them more willing to voice genuine weaknesses than asking directly.
Interviewers who model vulnerability first create the opening for a more honest answer.
Getting an accurate read on weaknesses is framed as just as essential to a hiring decision as assessing strengths.
quotes: In interview settings, candidates are so disinclined to describe their weaknesses that they often turn to the sleight-of-hand trick of describing the downside of one of their strengths.

Asking candidates to project what others might say is a way to break through the posturing of only putting their strengths forward.
They are more likely to be honest, or at least create an opening to explore their actual weaknesses, if they are asked to speak from the vantage those who know them well.
Good leaders work hard to get candidates talking about their weaknesses, too. They know that getting the full picture is critical to an accurate assessment.
